sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

You'll build a mental model for five concepts that will make you a better AI user for the rest of your life: **tokens**, **context windows**, **prediction**, **temperature**, and **training vs. runtime**. Understanding these isn't optional — they explain almost every quirk, limitation, and capability of every AI tool you'll ever use.

No math. No code. Just accurate mental models.

## The Core Idea: Next-Token Prediction

At the most fundamental level, a language model does one thing: **predict the most likely next token** given everything that came before it.

A **token** is roughly a word or word-fragment. The sentence *"The cat sat on the mat"* is about 7 tokens. Claude processes everything — your question, the conversation history, its instructions — as a sequence of tokens.

When you send Claude a message, it doesn't "think" the way humans do. It repeatedly runs one calculation: *given all the tokens so far, what token should come next?* It does this thousands of times per second to generate a response.

This sounds too simple to produce intelligent output. But trained on enough data, next-token prediction turns out to be a surprisingly deep skill. To predict what comes next in text about physics, medicine, code, or poetry, you have to implicitly learn a lot about physics, medicine, code, and poetry.

**The critical implication:** Claude doesn't "know" things the way you know your own name. It generates responses that are statistically likely given the training data. Usually that's right. Sometimes it's confidently wrong — which is what hallucination is.

**The cooking analogy:** A language model is like a chef who has eaten at a million restaurants. They don't have a rulebook for every cuisine — they've absorbed so many patterns that they can produce authentic-tasting food in any style. They're not *copying* recipes; they've internalised the underlying logic — and they can produce a dish they've never made before by combining patterns they have seen.

## Tokens — The Currency of AI

Tokens are how AI models measure and price everything. Understanding tokens makes you a better AI user and helps you understand costs if you ever build with the API.

**Token sizes:**
- 1 token ≈ 4 characters in English
- 1 token ≈ ¾ of a word
- 100 tokens ≈ 75 words
- 1,000 tokens ≈ 750 words ≈ 1.5 pages

**What gets tokenised:**
- Your question: tokens
- Previous messages in the conversation: tokens
- The system prompt (Claude's instructions): tokens
- Claude's response: tokens

All of these together must fit within the context window (see below).

**Why token boundaries matter:**
Some words are multiple tokens. "Unbelievable" might be split: "Un" + "believ" + "able". Numbers and code are often tokenised differently from prose. This is why AI sometimes makes odd errors mid-word — the model's prediction can go wrong at a token boundary.

**Tokens and cost:**
When you use the API (building your own tools), you pay per million tokens. A 1,000-token prompt costs 4× as much to send repeatedly as a 250-token prompt. This is why professional AI users think carefully about prompt length — not just for quality, but for cost.

## The Context Window — Working Memory

Every LLM has a **context window** — the maximum amount of text it can "see" and reason about at once. Think of it as the model's working memory.

Everything inside the context window, the model knows. Everything outside it, the model has no access to.

This is why:
- Claude doesn't remember your conversation from yesterday (that conversation is gone — outside the window)
- Very long documents can hit limits (the document might not fit in the window)
- Starting a new chat "resets" Claude (empty context = no memory of previous chats)

**Context windows in 2026:**
- Claude Sonnet 5 and Opus 4.8: 1,000,000 tokens on the API by default; Sonnet 5 also gets the full 1M on paid chat plans, while Opus 4.8 is capped at 500,000 tokens in the chat interface
- GPT-5.x family (OpenAI): up to 1,000,000 tokens on the flagship tier; the mini and nano tiers use smaller windows
- Gemini 3 Pro: 1,000,000 tokens (an entire year of dense reading), with Gemini 3 Flash offering a faster 200,000-token tier

Exact numbers shift every few months as vendors ship new versions — don't memorise these figures, memorise the *concept* and check the current spec when it matters for a real task.

**What fills the context window:**
At any point in a conversation, the context contains: the system prompt + all previous messages + the current message. Long conversations eat context, which is why very long chats sometimes produce less sharp responses — the model's working memory is filling up.

**Practical implication:** If you want Claude to remember something across sessions, you have to give it that information yourself. Paste it in, upload a file, or use Claude's Projects feature to persist context.

**The information order effect:** Claude (and all LLMs) tends to pay more attention to information at the beginning and end of the context window. If you have a long document and a specific question, put your question *first*, before the document — not after it. This is counterintuitive (humans usually read context then ask questions) but produces better AI results.

## Temperature — Controlling Creativity vs. Consistency

When an AI model predicts the next token, it generates a probability distribution over all possible tokens. Temperature is a parameter that controls how the model samples from that distribution.

**Low temperature (close to 0):**
- The model almost always picks the most probable next token
- Output is consistent, predictable, and focused
- Use for: factual questions, code generation, formal writing, tasks where you want the same answer each time

**High temperature (close to 1 or above):**
- The model samples more broadly, occasionally picking lower-probability tokens
- Output is more varied, creative, and surprising — but less reliable
- Use for: brainstorming, creative writing, generating options

In Claude.ai (the consumer interface), you don't control temperature directly — Anthropic sets it for you at a sensible default. But if you use the Claude API, you can set it explicitly. Understanding temperature helps explain why:
- The same question can get slightly different answers in different conversations (sampling variation)
- AI sometimes produces unexpected word choices (temperature lets lower-probability tokens occasionally "win")
- Some AI outputs are remarkably consistent while others vary noticeably

**The determinism myth:** Many people assume AI is deterministic — same input, same output. It's usually not. Temperature-based sampling means the same prompt generates slightly different responses. Some developers set temperature to 0 for fully deterministic output (useful for automated testing), but this makes the output more robotic.

## Training vs. Runtime — Two Completely Different Things

There are two distinct phases of an AI model's life:

**Training** — The model learns by processing billions of documents and adjusting its internal parameters to get better at next-token prediction. This happens once (or periodically at massive cost). You don't control this.

**Runtime (inference)** — When you send a message, the trained model uses its learned parameters to generate a response. This is what happens every time you use Claude. It's much cheaper and faster than training.

**Why this distinction matters:**
- The model's *knowledge* comes from training (has a cutoff date)
- The model's *behaviour* in a conversation depends on what's in the context window at runtime
- You can dramatically change what the model does at runtime using the context window — without changing the model itself
- This is what "prompting" is: runtime-level instruction that shapes behaviour without changing training

**What RLHF is (and why Claude isn't just a raw language model):**
Raw language models are capable but wild — they'll generate anything, helpful or not. Anthropic trains Claude with **Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF)**: human raters evaluate responses and score them for helpfulness, accuracy, and safety. The model is then trained to prefer responses humans rated highly.

This is why Claude is *helpful* (not just capable), declines harmful requests, and hedges appropriately when uncertain. The core model is the same; RLHF shaped how it uses that core capability.

## System Prompts — The Invisible Instructions

Every conversation with Claude has three layers:
1. **System prompt** — Instructions set by whoever deployed Claude (Anthropic, an app, a company) before you ever send a message. Invisible to you.
2. **Your messages** — What you type.
3. **Claude's responses** — What Claude generates.

The system prompt is powerful: it can tell Claude to adopt a persona, restrict what topics it will discuss, specify a response format, provide background context, or change how it behaves. When you use Claude.ai directly, Anthropic sets the system prompt. When a company integrates Claude into their product, *they* set the system prompt — which is why the same underlying model behaves differently in different apps.

**Why this matters for you as a user:**
- If Claude behaves oddly in a particular app, it might be following a system prompt you can't see
- When you build with the Claude API (later in this course), you'll write your own system prompts
- Understanding that a system prompt exists helps explain why the same question gets different answers in different Claude products

**You can simulate a system prompt** in Claude.ai by putting instructions at the start of your very first message in a conversation. This isn't as reliable as an actual system prompt, but it works well enough for most use cases.

sections.title: The Context Window Experiment + Temperature Discovery
sections.content:
Two experiments in one — both make concepts visceral and unforgettable.

**Experiment 1 — The Context Window (10 minutes)**

1. Open [Claude.ai](https://claude.ai) and paste a long Wikipedia article (3,000+ words — try the article on "World War II" or "Climate change").
2. Ask Claude to summarise it in three bullet points. It will do it perfectly — the full article is in its context window.
3. Ask a specific question about a detail mentioned in the article (a date, a name, a specific event). It answers correctly.
4. Start a **brand new conversation** (click "New Chat"). Ask Claude the same specific question without pasting anything.
5. Notice that Claude either doesn't know the answer or gives a generic response. The article was never in *this* conversation's context window.

**Write two sentences:**
1. What the context window is (in your own words)
2. One practical implication for how you'll use AI going forward

**Experiment 2 — Temperature in Action (5 minutes)**

In the same conversation as Experiment 1, send this prompt three times (just hit the send button three times with the same text):
```
Give me a single creative metaphor for the concept of a 'context window'.
```

Are all three responses the same? Different? How different?

**Write one sentence:** What does the variation between responses tell you about how AI generation works?

**Experiment 3 — System Prompt Simulation (5 minutes)**

Start a new chat. As your *very first message* (before asking anything else), write:
```
For this conversation: You are a blunt, direct expert who gives opinions not options. You never hedge. When I ask a question, give me your clearest recommendation, not a list of considerations.
```

Then ask a question that normally produces a hedge-filled response: *"Should I learn Python or JavaScript first?"*

Compare the response to what you normally get without the instruction. Did the system-prompt-style instruction change the output?

sections.question: You paste a 5,000-word document into Claude and have a long conversation about it over 30 turns. Near the end of the conversation, you notice Claude's responses about the document seem less precise and sometimes miss details it got right earlier. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Claude gets tired and less accurate over long conversations
The conversation history has grown long enough to push some of the original document content toward the edges of the context window, where models pay less attention
The document is corrupted and Claude can no longer read it correctly
You need to upgrade to Claude Pro for long conversations
sections.explanation: As a conversation grows, all the previous messages accumulate and fill the context window. The original document is still there, but it may now be buried under dozens of conversation turns. LLMs tend to attend more strongly to recent context and less to earlier context that's now far from the active position in the window. The fix: start a new conversation with the document fresh, or summarise the conversation so far and include that summary with the document in a new chat.

sections.title: Workshop A — Token Intuition Drill
sections.content:
Build a feel for tokens and why they matter — in under 10 minutes.

**Step 1 — Estimate before you measure.** Look at these three texts and guess how many tokens each contains:
- "Hello, how are you today?" (your guess: ___)
- A 100-word paragraph about climate change (your guess: ___)
- A 500-word email (your guess: ___)

Use the rule of thumb: 1 token ≈ ¾ of a word.

**Step 2 — Open [Claude.ai](https://claude.ai) and test your intuition.** Paste this prompt:
```
I want to understand how tokens work. Please tell me:
1. Roughly how many tokens are in the sentence: "Hello, how are you today?"
2. How does the word 'unbelievable' get tokenised — is it one token or multiple?
3. Why might numbers and code get tokenised differently from normal English words?
```

**Step 3 — The context window implications.** Now ask:
```
If a context window holds 200,000 tokens, roughly how many pages of a
typical novel would that fit? And how many back-and-forth exchanges in
a conversation before you start approaching that limit?
```

**Step 4 — Check your estimates.** How close were your guesses from Step 1?

**Step 5 — Ask Claude to review your understanding:**
```
I think I understand tokens now. Here's my mental model: [write 2-3 sentences
explaining what tokens are and why they matter]. What did I get right,
and what would you correct or add?
```

**The takeaway:** You now have an intuitive sense of the "cost" of AI interactions. Every prompt has a token price. Long conversations have a working-memory cost. This is the foundation for prompt efficiency — which you will practise throughout the course.

sections.title: Workshop B — Build Your Personal AI Cheat Sheet
sections.content:
You will create a one-page reference document called "How AI Actually Works" — your personal cheat sheet for the five core concepts from this lesson. This is something you will actually use: when you're unsure why AI is behaving strangely, when you're explaining AI to someone else, or when you come back to this course after a break.

**Step 1 — Open [Claude.ai](https://claude.ai). Start a new conversation and paste this prompt:**
```
I want to create a personal reference cheat sheet for how language models
work. Help me draft a one-page document that covers these five concepts in
plain English — as if explaining to someone smart but non-technical:

1. Next-token prediction (what the model is actually doing)
2. Tokens (what they are and why they matter)
3. Context window (what it is and the key practical implications)
4. Temperature (what it controls and when high/low matters)
5. Training vs. runtime (the difference and why it matters)

For each concept:
- One clear explanation (2-3 sentences)
- One practical implication for how I use AI day-to-day
- One common misconception to avoid

Format: clear headings, short paragraphs, no jargon. This should take under
2 minutes to read.
```

**Step 2 — Read the draft critically.** For each of the five sections, ask yourself: does this match what I actually learned in this lesson? If something seems off or too vague, note it.

**Step 3 — Request specific improvements.** For each section that needs work:
```
The section on [concept] isn't quite right. Specifically: [what's wrong or
missing]. Please revise that section.
```

**Step 4 — Add your own examples.** AI's examples are generic. For at least two of the five sections, ask Claude to help you add an example from YOUR context:
```
For the context window section, add an example relevant to someone who
[describe your job or main use case for AI]. Make it concrete and specific.
```

**Step 5 — The mandatory AI REVIEW step.** Paste your current draft and say:
```
Don't validate this — find 3 specific problems or gaps in this cheat
sheet. Consider: accuracy (anything technically wrong or oversimplified to
the point of being misleading?), usefulness (anything too vague to actually
help someone?), and completeness (what important nuance is missing?).
```

**Step 6 — Fix at least one problem** Claude identifies. If you disagree with the criticism, explain why — but engage with it.

**Step 7 — Format and save.** Open a new document (Google Docs, Word, or Notepad). Give it the title "How Language Models Work — My Reference". Add today's date. Copy your final cheat sheet in. Save it somewhere you can find it again.

**Step 8 — Quick self-test.** Close the document. Without looking, can you explain all five concepts in one sentence each? If not, re-read the sections you can't summarise. The goal isn't memorisation — it's understanding solid enough to explain.

**Your deliverable:** A personalised one-page reference document you can look up whenever AI behaves unexpectedly. You will reference this throughout the course.

**Why this approach works:** Writing the cheat sheet yourself (even with AI help) forces active engagement with the concepts. It's not enough to read — you have to decide what matters and put it in your own words. The adversarial review step ensures it's actually accurate, not just what sounds right.

sections.title: Workshop C — AI Review of a Conversation Gone Wrong
sections.content:
Recall a time when AI gave you a confusing, unhelpful, or unexpectedly bad response. If you can't think of one, run one of the prompts below deliberately. Then use AI to diagnose what went wrong — this builds the skill of understanding AI failures rather than just experiencing them.

**Option A — Use a real past experience.** Think of a time AI gave you a strange, unhelpful, or obviously wrong response. Write a brief description of what happened: what you asked, what you got, and why it was wrong or confusing.

**Option B — Create a failure deliberately.** Try one of these prompts in a new Claude.ai conversation and observe the result:
- Ask about a very recent news event (last week) — watch what happens when the training cutoff is relevant
- Ask Claude to tell you what's in a document without giving it the document — watch it hallucinate or refuse
- Ask the same complex question three times in a row — note the variation in responses

**Step 1 — Document the failure.** Write 2-3 sentences: what happened, and what surprised you about the response.

**Step 2 — Open a fresh Claude.ai conversation and paste this prompt:**
```
I want to understand why an AI interaction went wrong.

Here is what happened: [describe the failure — what you asked, what you got,
what was wrong or surprising]

Using what you know about how language models work — tokens, context windows,
training cutoffs, temperature, next-token prediction — what is the most likely
explanation for this behaviour? And what could I have done differently to get
a better result?
```

**Step 3 — Evaluate the diagnosis.** Does Claude's explanation make sense given what you learned in this lesson? Does it use the right concepts accurately?

**Step 4 — Ask a follow-up:** "What is one prompt technique that would reduce this kind of problem in the future?"

**Step 5 — Note the fix.** Write one sentence in your notes: the technique you'll try next time you run into this type of failure.

**Why this exercise works:** Most beginners learn AI by trial and error — they get bad results and try again. This exercise breaks that pattern by helping you build a causal model. When you understand *why* a failure happened, you can prevent it next time instead of just trying different random prompts.

sections.title: Workshop D — Real-World Application: Redesign a Real Prompt
sections.content:
Pick a real task you've recently used AI for — or something you've been meaning to try — and apply this lesson's concepts to make your prompt dramatically better.

**Step 1 — Pick your real task.** This should be something you genuinely need or recently tried. Examples:
- Asking AI to help you write an email
- Getting a summary of a long document
- Asking for help understanding a concept in your field
- Getting ideas for a project or presentation
- Asking for feedback on something you wrote

Write your original prompt (or best guess at the prompt you used) in your notes.

**Step 2 — Diagnose your original prompt** using what you learned in this lesson. Ask yourself:
- Is there a context window problem? (Did I give enough context? Too much?)
- Is there a training/runtime issue? (Am I asking about something after the training cutoff?)
- Is the temperature issue relevant? (Do I want consistent or creative output?)
- Am I using a system-prompt technique to shape the response?

**Step 3 — Open [Claude.ai](https://claude.ai) and paste:**
```
I have a task I want to use AI for, and I want to understand how to write
a much better prompt for it.

My task: [describe the task in plain terms]
My original prompt (or what I would have written): [paste your original prompt]

Using principles of how language models work — context window, token
efficiency, the role of upfront instructions — help me redesign this prompt
to get significantly better results. Explain what you changed and why.
```

**Step 4 — Test both versions.** In two separate conversations, run your original prompt and the redesigned prompt. Compare the outputs. Which is more useful? Why?

**Step 5 — Note your learning.** Write one sentence about the most impactful change in the redesigned prompt. This is the technique to remember.

**Your deliverable:** A better version of a real prompt you'll use again, plus an understanding of why it works better. This is applied knowledge — not abstract understanding, but a concrete improvement to something you actually do.

**The meta-principle:** Understanding how the tool works always leads to better use of the tool. Every concept in this lesson maps to a practical prompt improvement. Token awareness = concise, focused prompts. Context window awareness = knowing when to start fresh vs. continue. Training/runtime awareness = knowing what information to provide vs. what AI already knows.

sections.question: You ask Claude the same question twice in a row in two separate conversations and get noticeably different answers. Which explanation is most accurate?
options: Claude is inconsistent and unreliable — this is a bug
One conversation must have had different context affecting the response
Temperature-based sampling means the same prompt can produce different outputs across conversations — this is by design
The internet was different when you asked each time
sections.explanation: Temperature-based sampling is intentional — it introduces controlled variation so the model doesn't always pick the single most probable token. This is what makes AI creative and varied rather than robotic. The same prompt can legitimately produce different outputs. This is not a bug; it is a feature for creative tasks (brainstorming, writing) and a consideration for consistency-sensitive tasks (always review important outputs rather than assuming the same prompt gives the same result).

sections.question: You are helping a colleague who wants to use Claude to draft 50 similar emails with only small changes each time. They ask whether Claude will 'remember' the instructions from the first email when drafting the 50th. What do you tell them?
options: Yes — Claude stores instructions permanently once given
No — each conversation starts fresh. To apply consistent instructions to all 50 emails, include the instructions at the start of every conversation, or use Claude's Projects feature to persist them
It depends on whether they use Claude Free or Claude Pro
Yes — Claude's RLHF training means it adapts and remembers user preferences
sections.explanation: Claude has no memory between conversations. Each new chat starts with an empty context window — no knowledge of previous conversations. For recurring tasks with consistent instructions, the solution is to include those instructions every time (paste them at the start), use Claude Projects (which persist instructions across conversations in that project), or build a system prompt if using the API. RLHF shapes the model's general helpfulness during training — it does not give Claude memory of your specific instructions at runtime.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 1-2.** You now understand tokens, context windows, next-token prediction, temperature, the training/runtime distinction, RLHF, and system prompts. These five concepts explain almost every behaviour you'll observe in AI tools — both impressive capabilities and frustrating limitations.
